items.followUp: Two bodies of masses 2 kg and 3 kg move together at 4 m/s. Find their total momentum.

rubric.why: States the law and its condition.
rubric.description: Correctly states that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the total momentum being conserved and 1 mark for specifying that no external force acts on the system.

rubric.why: Explains conservation using the forces during an interaction.
rubric.description: Explains that the interaction forces are equal and opposite, so the changes in momentum are equal and opposite.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for equal and opposite interaction forces and 1 mark for the resulting equal and opposite momentum changes or unchanged total momentum.

modelAnswer: For an isolated system, if no external force acts on it, its total momentum remains constant.
During an interaction between two bodies, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite: F₁ = −F₂.
Since force is the rate of change of momentum, the changes in the bodies’ momenta are equal and opposite.
Therefore, the total momentum before interaction equals the total momentum after interaction: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.

items.followUp: State the first condition of equilibrium and explain how it applies to a body acted on by two forces.

rubric.description: Defines equilibrium in terms of the resultant force on a body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for saying the body is in equilibrium and 1 mark for stating that its resultant or net force is zero (or that it remains at rest or moves with constant velocity).

rubric.why: Assesses the first condition and its component form.
rubric.description: States that the vector sum of forces is zero and gives the component condition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the zero vector sum of forces and 1 mark for giving the component equations or explaining that forces balance.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force acting on it is zero; it then remains at rest or moves with constant velocity.
The first condition of equilibrium is that the vector sum of all forces acting on the body is zero: ΣF = 0.
In two dimensions, this requires ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣFᵧ = 0.
Thus, the forces acting in opposite directions balance one another.

items.followUp: A hydraulic press has piston areas of 0.02 m² and 0.50 m². If a force of 100 N is applied to the small piston, find the force on the large piston.

rubric.why: Assesses the statement of Pascal’s law.
rubric.description: States that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished throughout the fluid and to the container walls.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the applied pressure in an enclosed fluid and 1 mark for stating that it is transmitted equally or undiminished.

rubric.why: Assesses the pressure relation used in a hydraulic press.
rubric.description: Relates pressure, force and piston area for both pistons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly writing pressure as force divided by area for the two pistons.

rubric.description: Uses equal pressure at the two pistons to derive the force-area equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for equating the pressures and obtaining a correct equivalent equation.

modelAnswer: Pascal’s law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished in every direction throughout the fluid and to the walls of its container.
In a hydraulic press, let F₁ and A₁ be the force and area of the small piston, and F₂ and A₂ those of the large piston.
By Pascal’s law, the pressures at the pistons are equal: P₁ = P₂.
Since pressure P = F/A, F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
Therefore, F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁.

items.followUp: Define derived quantities and give two examples.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of base quantities.
rubric.description: Defines base quantities as independent quantities not defined in terms of other physical quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the idea that base quantities are independent or cannot be expressed in terms of other quantities.

rubric.description: Gives two valid examples of base quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two valid examples, such as length, mass or time.

modelAnswer: Base quantities are independent physical quantities that are not defined in terms of other physical quantities.
Examples include length and mass.

items.followUp: What is the zero error of a measuring instrument, and how can it affect a measurement?

rubric.why: Assesses the meaning of zero error.
rubric.description: Defines zero error as a nonzero instrument reading when the actual measured quantity is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for referring to the instrument’s reading when the actual quantity is zero and 1 mark for stating that this reading is not zero.

modelAnswer: Zero error is the nonzero reading shown by a measuring instrument when the actual value of the quantity being measured is zero.
It occurs when the instrument does not read zero at its zero position.

items.followUp: A car travels 60 m east in 3 s. What is its uniform velocity?

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of uniform velocity.
rubric.description: States that uniform velocity means equal displacements in equal time intervals in the same direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for equal displacement in equal time intervals and 1 mark for the same direction or constant direction.

modelAnswer: An object has uniform velocity when it makes equal displacements in equal intervals of time in the same direction.
Thus, both its speed and direction remain constant.

items.followUp: According to Galileo, what happens to the acceleration of a heavy and a light object falling freely in the absence of air resistance?

rubric.why: Assesses Galileo’s view of freely falling bodies.
rubric.description: States that all freely falling bodies have the same acceleration, irrespective of their masses, when air resistance is absent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that freely falling bodies have the same acceleration or fall at the same rate, and 1 mark for noting that this is independent of mass (or that air resistance is neglected).

modelAnswer: Galileo’s view was that, in the absence of air resistance, all bodies falling freely have the same acceleration.
Their acceleration does not depend on their masses.

items.followUp: A 0.5 kg object moves in a circle of radius 2 m at 4 m/s. Calculate the centripetal force.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of centripetal force.
rubric.description: Defines centripetal force as the force directed towards the centre of a circular path that keeps the object moving in that path.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the force as directed towards the centre of the circular motion.

rubric.why: Assesses the formula for centripetal force.
rubric.description: Gives the correct formula for centripetal force.

modelAnswer: Centripetal force is the force directed towards the centre of a circular path that keeps an object moving in that path.
Its formula is F = mv²/r.
